1.title: Incident Response and Investigations
1.text: Welcome to Module seventeen: Incident Response and Investigations. It covers the exam area Security Operations. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. four point seven Summarize concepts associated with incident response activities. four point eight Given a scenario, use data, artifacts and sources to support a security investigation. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Security Operations (twenty-seven percent). Exam format: up to ninety questions in ninety minutes; a score of seven hundred fifty on a scale of one hundred to nine hundred passes. Validated against: the official Comp T I A Security plus S Y zero eight oh one V eight exam objectives.

1.title: The incident response process
1.text: The incident response process. The figure shows this: Incident response phases from preparation to post-incident review.

1.title: The incident response process, continued
1.text: The incident response process. Preparation. What happens: Be ready before an incident. Key items: Training, testing, tabletop exercises (discussion-based walk-through), playbooks (step-by-step guides), simulations, roles. Identification. What happens: Detect and confirm an incident. Key items: Detection, internal and external advisories, threat hunting (actively searching for hidden threats). Investigation. What happens: Find what happened. Key items: Digital forensics, chain of custody, e-discovery, preservation.

1.title: The incident response process, continued
1.text: The incident response process. Containment. What happens: Stop the spread. Key items: Quarantine and isolation of affected systems. Negotiation. What happens: Dealing with an attacker (for example ransom) when decided by leadership. Key items: Involve legal and executives. Eradication and recovery. What happens: Remove the cause and restore systems. Key items: Remove malware, patch, rebuild, restore from clean backups.

1.title: The incident response process, continued
1.text: The incident response process. Notification and external reporting. What happens: Tell the right parties. Key items: Stakeholders, customers, law enforcement, mandatory reporting. Post-incident. What happens: Learn and improve. Key items: Lessons learned, root cause analysis, post-incident reporting (P I R). Exam tip: The order is prepare, identify, contain, eradicate, recover, learn. Containment comes before eradication: stop the spread first, then remove. Lessons learned feed back into preparation.

1.title: Preparation and exercises
1.text: Preparation and exercises. Tabletop exercise. People talk through a scenario; low cost, no systems touched. Simulation. Hands-on test with a realistic attack. Playbook. Documented steps for a specific incident type. Roles. Incident commander, communications, technical lead, legal.

1.title: Digital forensics concepts
1.text: Digital forensics concepts. Digital forensics. Collecting and analyzing digital evidence in a sound way. Chain of custody. A record of who handled the evidence, when and why, so it stays trustworthy in court. Preservation. Keep evidence unchanged (write blockers, copies, legal hold). E-discovery. Finding and producing electronic records for legal matters. Order of volatility. Collect most volatile first: memory, then temporary files, then disk, then logs and archives.

1.title: Digital forensics concepts, continued
1.text: Digital forensics concepts. The figure shows this: Order of volatility: capture memory first, then disk, then remote logs and archives.

1.title: Data, artifacts and sources for investigations
1.text: Data, artifacts and sources for investigations. Log types. Access and accounting (logical, physical), device, server, application, authentication, communication, audit, endpoint, network, metadata. Data sources. Vulnerability scans, automated reports, net flow or I P fix, surveillance footage, security tools, dashboards, packet captures. File and log integrity. Hashes and protection show that evidence is unchanged. System image. Memory dump, bit-level copy, snapshot. Stakeholders. Human Resources, accounts, legal are involved when staff or money is concerned. Log-parsing techniques. Searching, filtering and correlating logs to find the story. Exam tip: A bit-level (forensic) copy keeps deleted data and slack space; a normal copy does not. Always hash the evidence and the copy. Metadata (who, when, where) is often enough to build a timeline.

1.title: Data, artifacts and sources for investigations, continued
1.text: Data, artifacts and sources for investigations. Exam tip: Chain of custody records who handled evidence; the order of volatility says to collect memory first, then disk, then logs and archives.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Fabrikam Outdoors finds ransomware spreading across its file servers. What should the team do first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Contain the affected systems by isolating them. Containment stops the spread before eradication and recovery begin.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Leadership wants to rehearse a data breach by discussing roles and decisions around a table, without touching systems. Which exercise fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Tabletop exercise. A tabletop exercise walks through a scenario in discussion form.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An investigator logs who collected a laptop, who held it and when it was transferred. What does this protect? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Chain of custody. Chain of custody records evidence handling so it stays trustworthy.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A responder must capture evidence from a running server. Which item should be collected first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Memory contents. Volatile data such as memory is lost first, so it is collected before disk and archives.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. After an incident, the team meets to document what went wrong and how to improve. Which phase is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Post-incident, lessons learned. Reviewing the incident to improve is the lessons learned and root cause part of the post-incident phase.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Which source shows who talked to whom on the network and how much data moved, even without packet contents? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: net flow or I P fix. Flow records summarize network conversations and are useful for timelines.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Name the phases of incident response in the objectives. Answer: Preparation, identification, investigation, containment, negotiation, eradication and recovery, notification, post-incident. Question two. What is a playbook? Answer: A documented set of steps for a specific type of incident. Question three. What is threat hunting? Answer: Actively searching for threats that have evaded detection.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What does chain of custody document? Answer: Who handled the evidence, when and why. Question five. What is a bit-level copy? Answer: An exact copy of every bit of a drive, including deleted data. Question six. What does P I R stand for? Answer: Post-incident reporting.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Phases: prepare, identify, investigate, contain, negotiate, eradicate and recover, notify, post-incident (lessons learned, root cause). Exercises: tabletop (talk), simulation (hands-on), playbooks, roles. Forensics: digital forensics, chain of custody, preservation, e-discovery, order of volatility. Sources: log types, vulnerability scans, net flow or I P fix, footage, packet captures, hashes, memory dump, bit-level copy, snapshot. In the next module, we continue the course.
